Abstract
Recent advances in embodied artificial intelligence (EAI) have un-
leashed new potential in many frontiers. Current EAI systems of-
ten combine vision-language-action (VLA) inference with high-
frequency model predictive control (MPC). On mobile GPUs, these
workloads are typically serialized, causing control deadline misses.
We present Dubot, a framework that automatically schedules
VLA inference and MPC on a single mobile GPU. Specifically,
Dubot identifies concurrent opportunities and proposes three co-
location mechanisms: spatial partitioning, block-level co-location,
and intra-block fusion. By leveraging different mechanisms, Dubot
enables fine-grained co-location to improve the efficiency of various
VLA-MPC operator pairs. Dubot further proposes a co-location op-
timizer that can determine the optimal co-location schedule under
workload dependency, QoS requirements, and hardware-resource
constraints. Across representative VLA inference paradigms on
NVIDIA Jetson Orin and Thor, Dubot achieves up to 1.4× end-to-
end speedup and reduces QoS violations by up to 38%.
Keywords
VLA-MPC Control, Robotic Runtime Optimization.
1
Introduction
Embodied artificial intelligence (EAI) has rapidly moved toward
real-world deployment in humanoid robots [13, 22, 23], autonomous
vehicles [29, 33, 63], and more [4, 11, 14]. Recent vision-language-
action (VLA) models [7, 12, 17, 18, 36, 37, 40, 56] have substantially
improved a robot’s ability to understand natural language and
generate task-level actions under dynamic or unseen environments.
However, an EAI system is more than a VLA model. In practice,
an EAI system consists of a hierarchical control stack with two
tightly coupled control loops [47] (Sec. 2.1). At the higher level,
∗Corresponding Authors.
ISCA ’27, Atlanta, Georgia, USA
2027. ACM ISBN 978-x-xxxx-xxxx-x/YY/MM
https://doi.org/XXXXXXX.XXXXXXX
a VLA model periodically consumes an instruction and the latest
sensory observation to predict an action horizon, i.e., a short se-
quence of actions. At the lower level, a model predictive control
(MPC) algorithm continuously converts these high-level actions
into fine-grained actuator signals. Moreover, the lower-level con-
troller needs to incorporate recent states, motion constraints, and
obstacle information to maintain a safe and smooth trajectory.
These two control levels operate at different frequencies. VLA in-
ference is compute-intensive but is typically invoked at a relatively
low frequency, e.g., 20–60 Hz [2, 36, 40]. In contrast, the low-level
controller must respond rapidly to changes in the robot state and its
environment. Depending on the platform and actuator, the control
frequency can reach 500 Hz [16, 26, 49]. Meeting low-level control
deadlines is often the primary runtime requirement, since deadline
misses can introduce trajectory jitter or unsafe behaviors.
Issue. Conceptually, these two loops can execute concurrently.
After the VLA model predicts an action horizon, the controller can
continuously optimize and execute the current trajectory while
the VLA model processes a new observation. In practice, however,
existing implementations have to execute the two workloads se-
quentially due to resource constraints, since these mobile platforms,
e.g., Nvidia Jetson Orin [50] and Thor [51], often have less compute
capacity than workstation GPUs. Sec. 7.1 shows that sequential
execution can lead to severe quality-of-service (QoS) violations.
Opportunity. Although VLA and MPC operate at different
frequencies, their dependencies do not require the two control loops
to remain serialized. Once a VLA action becomes available, MPC
can continuously generate control commands using the latest robot
state while subsequent VLA inference can proceed. This naturally
creates opportunities to overlap the two workloads.
Moreover, VLA and MPC require different GPU resources. VLA
inference is dominated by dense tensor operations that primarily
utilize Tensor cores, whereas MPC consists mainly of small ma-
trix and vector operations executed on CUDA cores (Sec. 3). Their
complementary execution characteristics create opportunities for
fine-grained co-location on the same GPU.
1

Zeyu Guo et al.
Challenge. However, efficiently co-locating VLA and MPC is
a scheduling problem that must account for both control depen-
dencies and GPU resource constraints. First, MPC jobs have strict
deadlines and depend on the VLA-generated actions. Their exe-
cution must be scheduled within the available overlap windows.
Second, different VLA operators exhibit distinct resource demands.
Thus, co-location performance depends heavily on the execution
mechanism and GPU resource allocation. All these factors together
determine the overall VLA-MPC execution performance.
Framework. To address these challenges, we introduce Dubot,
a framework for jointly orchestrating VLA inference and MPC com-
putation on a single GPU (Sec. 4). Given a VLA model, an MPC
algorithm, a target MPC frequency, and a target platform, Dubot
first identifies the execution windows in which MPC jobs can over-
lap with VLA stages based on their data dependencies. It then
constructs hardware-feasible co-location strategies for different
VLA operators. Lastly, Dubot jointly determines the co-location
mechanism and MPC workload assignment for each VLA stage,
minimizing VLA inference latency while satisfying MPC QoS.
VLA-MPC Co-Location. Dubot exposes different co-location
mechanisms to different VLA operators based on their resource
demands. For linear operations, we observe that linear operations
account for most of the VLA execution time and primarily use
Tensor cores, while MPC kernels mainly use CUDA cores. Dubot
considers three mechanisms where supported by the target GPU:
spatial partitioning, stream-based block-level co-location, and warp-
specialized intra-block fusion (Sec. 4.3). For a linear-MPC operation
pair, the best co-location mechanism depends on both the GPU
architecture and workload characteristics. For attention and non-
linear operations, Dubot restricts co-location to spatial partitioning
to reduce contention for SM-local resources. To let the optimizer
vary the amount of MPC work paired with each VLA operation,
Dubot groups consecutive QP iterations and partitions MPPI sam-
ples into independent path groups.
Co-Location Optimization. Given various co-location mech-
anisms, Dubot proposes an optimizer in Sec. 5 that formulates
the VLA-MPC co-location mapping as a constrained optimization
problem. For each candidate mechanism, Dubot first uses offline-
calibrated performance models to estimate the co-location latency
of the VLA stage and its assigned MPC (Sec. 5.1). Using these esti-
mates, Dubot selects the co-location mechanism and GPU resource
allocation for each VLA stage and determines the number of QP
iterations or MPPI paths to assign to it (Sec. 5.2). By solving the
constrained optimization, Dubot automatically minimizes VLA
inference latency subject to workload dependencies, GPU resource
constraints, and MPC QoS requirements.
Results. We evaluate Dubot on two robotic platforms, Nvidia
Jetson Orin [50] and Thor [51], across three widely adopted VLA
inference paradigms [36, 37, 40]. Compared with the sequential
baseline, Dubot improves end-to-end EAI performance by up to
1.4× and reduces QoS violations by up to 38%. Compared with prior
co-location strategies [77, 86], Dubot achieves up to 1.3× speedup.
In summary, this paper makes the following contributions:
• We characterize end-to-end EAI execution on mobile GPUs
and expose the potential co-location opportunities between
VLA inference and high-frequency MPC computation.

• We propose an operator-aware co-location framework that
exploits complementary GPU resources through spatial par-
titioning, block-level co-location, and intra-block fusion.
• We formulate VLA–MPC orchestration as a constrained op-
timization and develop an efficient scheduling solver.
• Dubot achieves up to 1.4× end-to-end speedup and 38%
fewer QoS violations over the GPU baselines.
2
Background
This section provides the necessary background for EAI systems.
We first introduce the control pipeline of an EAI system with two
tightly coupled control loops (Sec. 2.1). We then explain representa-
tive VLA inference paradigms in Sec. 2.2. Lastly, we introduce two
widely used MPC solvers, QP- and MPPI-based MPC, in Sec. 2.3.
2.1
Embodied AI Systems
As shown in Fig. 1, an EAI system typically consists of two tightly
coupled control loops: a high-level planning loop and a low-level
control loop. The high-level loop is responsible for understand-
ing task instructions and predicting future actions in the current
environment. It commonly executes a VLA model, which takes a
natural language instruction, I, together with the latest sensory ob-
servations, o𝑡, as input and predicts a short horizon, i.e., a sequence
of high-level actions, {a𝑡}. Within each iteration, the VLA model
includes new sensory observations to generate updated actions.
The goal of the low-level control loop is to translate the action
sequence {a𝑡} predicted by the VLA model into executable actuator
commands. Unlike the high-level loop, which primarily focuses on
short-horizon planning, the low-level loop must account for robot
dynamics, actuator constraints, and nearby obstacles. Its objective
is to ensure that the planned actions can be executed safely and
smoothly without exceeding the motor limits or destabilizing the
system, e.g., causing the robot to fall. Therefore, the low-level MPC
algorithm continuously refines the high-level action sequence and
generates control signals that can be directly issued to the actuators.
Both control loops operate iteratively but at substantially differ-
ent frequencies. E.g., the high-level loop typically runs at 20–60 Hz [2,
40], whereas the low-level loop executes at a much higher frequency,
200-500 Hz [16, 26]. This hierarchical organization allows the robot
to combine the semantic reasoning of VLA models with the respon-
siveness and safety guarantees of conventional MPC algorithms.

2.2
VLA Models
VLA models serve as the high-level policies to predict short-horizon
future actions in an EAI system. However, existing VLA models [45,
90] have different action generation paradigms. Each offers trade-
offs between efficiency and task accuracy. We classify their infer-
ence processes into three representative paradigms: autoregressive-
based [17, 36, 56], prefill-only-based [37], and diffusion-based [18,
28, 40] inference. Despite these differences, existing baseline EAI
systems generally execute VLA inference and MPC computation,
denoted by M, sequentially on the GPU, as shown in Fig. 2.
Autoregressive VLA. Fig. 2a shows the pipeline of autoregres-
sive (AR)-based VLA inference. Each inference starts with a prefill
stage that encodes the instruction and visual observations. The
model then enters a decoding stage. In this stage, the VLA model
generates action tokens one at a time. Because each decoding step
depends on previously generated tokens, the decoding process must
execute sequentially. One action is often represented by multiple to-
kens, e.g., an arm action is encoded by seven tokens [36]. Different
VLAs could have different action encoding schemes [82]. Once a
complete action is generated, the sequential baseline pauses VLA de-
coding and invokes MPC to refine the action into low-level controls.
Decoding resumes after the scheduled MPC work completes.
Prefill-Only VLA. Fig. 2b shows the pipeline of prefill-only (PO)-
based VLA inference. A PO-based VLA model predicts a short action
chunk in a single prefill stage without a subsequent autoregressive
decoding stage. Consequently, PO-based inference is dominated
by highly parallel tensor kernels, e.g., linear operations. Once an
action chunk has been generated, the MPC controller processes it
to produce low-level controls before the next VLA inference.
Diffusion-Based VLA. Fig. 2c shows the pipeline of diffusion-
based VLA inference. A diffusion-based VLA model starts from a
noisy action sequence and iteratively refines it through 𝑁denoising
steps. During each step, the model generates an updated action
prediction conditioned on the instruction and visual observations.
As shown in Fig. 2c, all actions within one denoising step can be
processed in parallel. However, consecutive denoising steps must
execute sequentially because each step depends on the output of
the previous one. Once the denoising process completes, the result
action chunk is then passed to the MPC controller. Similar to PO-
based VLAs, existing systems execute MPC after VLA inference.
Sequential VLA-MPC Execution. Across all three inference
paradigms, existing EAI systems treat VLA and MPC as separate
GPU workloads and execute them sequentially. This execution

model essentially serializes two control loops on a single resource-
constrained mobile GPU. As we show in Sec. 4, this serialization
can leave significant GPU resources underutilized, which motivates
us to overlap VLA with MPC to reduce end-to-end EAI latency.
2.3
MPC Algorithms
As discussed in Sec. 2.1, MPC serves as the low-level controller in an
EAI system. As shown in Fig. 3, given the current robot state, s𝑡, and
a reference action sequence, {a𝑡}, from a VLA model, MPC predicts
the robot motion over a short horizon and searches for a sequence
of control inputs that can best track the reference trajectory. Unlike
the VLA model, which generates high-level actions, MPC must
account for robot dynamics, motor limits, collision constraints, and
more [3]. Once the MPC generates a sequence of control inputs,
only the first control input of the optimized sequence is issued to
the actuators. At the next control cycle, the MPC then incorporates
the latest robot state and repeats the optimization. This enables the
controller to respond rapidly to changes in the robot state and its
environment until the target destination is reached.
Existing MPC algorithms employ different optimization solvers.
In general, these solvers can be broadly classified into two represen-
tative paradigms: quadratic-programming (QP)-based MPC [10, 46]
and model predictive path integral (MPPI)-based MPC [75, 76].
QP-based MPC repeatedly solves a constrained optimization prob-
lem, whereas MPPI-based MPC searches for a control sequence
by sampling and evaluating candidate trajectories. The following
paragraphs explain their basic workflows and characteristics.
QP-Based MPC. This type of MPC solver reformulates low-
level control as a constrained optimization over a finite prediction
horizon. Given the initial robot state s0 and a reference trajectory

QP solvers refine the control sequence through iterative opti-
mization, which is inherently sequential. Within each iteration,
however, operations, e.g., robot-state propagation, residual com-
putation, and variable updates, expose data-level parallelism. For
instance, OSQP [65] accelerates convex QPs by exploiting SIMD
vector instructions. Its GPU counterpart, cuOSQP [60], maps the
dominant sparse matrix and vector operations onto CUDA cores to
achieve higher parallelism.
MPPI-Based MPC. This class of MPC algorithms does not di-
rectly solve a constrained optimization problem. Instead, MPPI
approximates the solution by sampling and evaluating a large num-
ber of candidate control sequences. Given the current robot state,
s0, and a reference control sequence, {uref

Although the computation within each trajectory is sequential
across timesteps, different sampled trajectories are mutually inde-
pendent and can be evaluated in parallel. Existing GPU implementa-
tions [75, 76] therefore map trajectories to different CUDA threads
or thread blocks and use parallel reductions to aggregate their costs
and update the control sequence. Thus, MPPI-based MPC exposes
path-level parallelism and is well suited to GPU execution.
3
Motivation
In this section, we explain the need to jointly optimize VLA in-
ference and MPC computation in an end-to-end EAI system. We
first show that both workloads take non-trivial time in the overall
execution. We then characterize their GPU execution behaviors
and show the opportunity for concurrent execution.
Execution Breakdown. Fig. 4 shows the execution breakdown
of seven representative end-to-end EAI workloads across different
VLA inference paradigms and MPC solvers. We measure their la-
tency on a mobile SoC, Nvidia Orin [50], where VLA inference and
low-level MPC computation are executed sequentially. Both VLA
(a) VLA inference with QP-based MPC.
(b) VLA inference with MPPI-based MPC.
Fig. 4: The execution breakdown of seven mainstream VLA
models [17, 18, 28, 36, 37, 40, 56] with two MPCs [10, 76] on
Orin SoC [50]. (a) QP-based MPCs; (b) MPPI-based MPCs.
(a) Nvidia Orin SoC.
(b) Nvidia Thor SoC.
Fig. 5: The operator-level breakdown of VLA models [17, 18,
28, 36, 37, 40, 56] on two Nvidia mobile SoCs, Orin [50] and
Thor [51]. Linear operations are the main bottlenecks.
(a) Nvidia Orin SoC.
(b) Nvidia Thor SoC.
Fig. 6: The operator breakdown of two MPC algorithms [10,
76] on two Nvidia mobile SoCs, Orin [50] and Thor [51].
inference and MPC computations take non-trivial execution time.
For instance, with the QP-based MPC, VLA inference and MPC
account for 57% and 43% of the end-to-end latency, respectively.
Although each MPC execution is relatively lightweight, its high
frequency makes its cumulative execution non-trivial.
The result shows that accelerating only VLAs leaves a substantial
fraction of the end-to-end runtime untouched. Moreover, simply
interleaving the two workloads can delay latency-critical MPC
execution and lead to severe QoS violations. Thus, improving end-
to-end performance requires optimizing both VLA and MPC.
Workload Characteristics. Although VLA inference and MPC
computation both execute on the GPU, they show different compu-
tational characteristics. VLA is dominated by dense matrix multi-
plications, which are typically mapped to Tensor cores rather than
general-purpose CUDA cores. Fig. 5 shows the breakdown of differ-
ent operators in VLA models. For instance, on Orin SoC [50], linear
layers in VLA models account for 80% of the VLA execution time
and primarily consist of compute-intensive matrix multiplications.
In contrast, MPC algorithms are predominantly executed on
CUDA cores. For instance, QP-based MPC mainly consists of sparse
matrix-vector multiplications, residual computations, and iterative
variable updates. MPPI-based MPC propagates robot states and
evaluates costs across a large number of sampled trajectories. These
operations often involve small tensor shapes and element-wise
computation. Fig. 6 shows the execution time breakdown of MPC
algorithms on two SoCs. On average, matrix-vector and element-
wise operations take 96% of the total MPC execution time. Thus,
MPC workloads are more suitable for CUDA cores.

Fig. 7: Overview of the Dubot framework. Dubot con-
structs VLA stages and MPC work groups, then enumerates
hardware-feasible co-location configurations by VLA opera-
tor class. The performance model estimates VLA-stage and
MPC-chunk completion times for each candidate. The opti-
mizer uses these estimates to select stage configurations and
map MPC work to VLA stages while respecting dependencies,
GPU resource reservations, and MPC deadlines.
Naturally, the execution characteristics of these two workloads
create a co-location opportunity. While a VLA kernel occupies
the Tensor cores, MPC computations can use otherwise idle CUDA
cores. Overlapping the two workloads can potentially increase GPU
utilization and reduce end-to-end latency without additional hard-
ware resources. One caveat is that Tensor cores and CUDA cores
are not fully independent: they still share streaming multiproces-
sor (SM) resources, e.g., registers and shared memory. Effectively
orchestrating their execution is key to the overall performance.
Summary. End-to-end EAI systems exhibit two key character-
istics. First, both the VLA loop and the high-frequency MPC loop
contribute non-trivially to the overall execution latency. Second,
the two workloads often rely on different GPU execution resources:
VLAs primarily use Tensor cores, whereas MPCs mainly use CUDA
cores. Together, these characteristics motivate fine-grained concur-
rent execution to improve end-to-end EAI.
4
Dubot Framework
The goal of Dubot is to improve the overall VLA performance
while preserving the QoS of MPC controls. To achieve this goal,
this section first describes the possible mechanisms that overlap
these two workloads (Sec. 4.3). Then, we describe the eligible co-
location mechanisms for different VLA operators (Sec. 4.4).
4.1
Overview
Fig. 7 gives an overview of Dubot. Given a VLA and an MPC algo-
rithm, a target control frequency, and a GPU platform, Dubot au-
tomatically derives a VLA-MPC co-location schedule that improves
VLA efficiency while satisfying the QoS of the MPC controller.
Dubot consists of three major components. First, Dubot iden-
tifies the execution windows in which high-frequency MPC can
overlap with subsequent VLA inference, as described in Sec. 4.2.
These opportunities depend on the inference paradigm of the VLA
model and the dependencies between the two control loops.
(a) Autoregressive (AR)-based VLA inference.
(b) Preﬁll-only (PO)-based VLA inference.

Fig. 8: Co-location opportunities between VLA inference

Second, Dubot constructs candidate co-location configurations
based on the resource characteristics of each VLA operator. As
shown in Sec. 4.3 and Sec. 4.4, Dubot considers three co-location
mechanisms: spatial partitioning, block-level co-location, and intra-
block fusion. Linear operations can use all three mechanisms, while
attention and non-linear operations use spatial partitioning to avoid
contention with latency-critical MPC computation. Meanwhile, QP
and MPPI workloads are partitioned into schedulable chunks, i.e.,
iteration groups and sampled-path groups, respectively.
Finally, Dubot proposes the co-location optimizer in Sec. 5 to
determine the execution configuration of each VLA stage and the
co-location placement of MPC computation across the VLA timeline.
The optimizer then uses offline performance models to estimate
candidate execution latencies and minimizes the end-to-end VLA
inference latency while enforcing constraints, e.g., MPC deadlines,
workload dependencies, and GPU resources. The final output speci-
fies the co-location mechanism, resource configuration, and kernel
mapping between MPC and VLA.
4.2
VLA-MPC Co-Location Opportunities
Opportunities. Although existing EAI systems execute VLA and
MPC sequentially, their dependencies do not require these two
control loops to remain serialized throughout execution. Once a
VLA model produces the action required by the low-level controller,
the corresponding MPC computation can proceed while subsequent
VLA inference can continue. Each VLA invocation uses the latest
available observation, while MPC continuously generates control
commands using the current robot state and the latest available
reference trajectory. Once a new VLA action becomes available, the
reference is updated for subsequent MPC invocations. This creates
an opportunity to overlap the two control loops, as shown in Fig. 8.
Fig. 8 shows these overlap opportunities for the three representa-
tive VLA inference paradigms introduced in Sec. 2.2. For AR-based
VLA models, once a complete action becomes available during de-
coding, its MPC computation can overlap with subsequent decoding
steps. For PO-based VLA models, MPC computation associated with
the current action chunk can overlap with the next VLA inference.

Similarly, for diffusion-based VLA models, once the denoising pro-
cess produces an action chunk, its MPC computation can overlap
with subsequent diffusion inference. Although the available over-
lap windows differ across inference paradigms, all three expose
opportunities to execute VLA and MPC concurrently.
These overlap windows determine when MPC can execute con-
currently with VLA. However, the optimal way to achieve this
execution overlap depends on the resource characteristics of both
the VLA operator and the MPC within each window. We next in-
troduce the mechanisms exploited by Dubot in Sec. 4.3.
4.3
Co-Location Mechanisms
Given an overlap window between VLA inference and MPC com-
putation, the next question is how these two workloads should
be co-located. Here, Dubot considers three co-location mecha-
nisms with different granularities: spatial partitioning, block-level
co-location, and intra-block fusion. Fig. 9 shows their examples.
Spatial Partitioning. One approach to co-executing two work-
loads is to use existing GPU spatial partitioning tools, e.g., MPS [52],
to divide SMs between VLA and MPC. As shown in Fig. 9a, one SM
group executes VLA kernels while another executes MPC kernels.
Because the two workloads are isolated at the SM level, spatial
partitioning avoids direct contention for SM-local resources and
requires minimal kernel modification. However, it cannot exploit
complementary compute resources within the same SM. E.g., SMs
assigned to VLA may leave part of their CUDA cores underutilized,
while SMs assigned to MPC may leave Tensor cores idle.
Block-Level Co-Location. This mechanism keeps VLA and MPC
as separate GPU kernels while allowing thread blocks from the two
kernels to co-locate on the same SM. As shown in Fig. 9b, each
block preserves its original thread organization, register allocation,
shared-memory allocation, and synchronization domain. Separate
CUDA streams allow the GPU to launch blocks from another kernel
once all blocks of the first kernel have been issued; whenever an SM
has sufficient resources, blocks from the second kernel can be co-
located on that SM. If these two kernels’ blocks leverage different
compute units, this co-location can achieve the Tensor-CUDA core
overlap between VLA and MPC. Nevertheless, co-located blocks
still compete for shared SM resources. The achievable concurrency
depends on their block-level resource footprints.
Intra-Block Fusion. To exploit the parallelism between Tensor
cores and CUDA cores, another approach is to fuse VLA and MPC
computations into a single thread block, a.k.a. warp specialization
(WASP) [9]. Different warps within the thread block are assigned
to different workloads, allowing their execution to be coordinated
at a finer granularity. Prior studies, e.g., Tacker [86], partition the
threads of a fused block into two groups: one performs Tensor core
computation, while the other performs general-purpose CUDA-
core computation. This mechanism provides fine-grained control
over synchronization, resource sharing, and execution order within
a block. However, intra-block fusion must accommodate the exe-
cution state and on-chip resource requirements of both workloads,
which can increase register and shared-memory pressure. It also re-
quires additional synchronization and kernel restructuring. Recent
GPU architectures [54] provide mechanisms, e.g., register reallo-
cation via setmaxnreg and asynchronous execution support, that
can reduce some of the overheads for warp-specialized pipelines.
4.4
VLA-MPC Co-Location Strategy
In Sec. 3, we show that different VLA operators exhibit differ-
ent GPU resource characteristics. Therefore, applying a single co-
location mechanism throughout VLA execution can either leave
GPU resources underutilized or introduce contention that causes
MPC to miss its QoS deadline. Here, Dubot adopts different co-
location mechanisms for VLA operators.
Linear Operations. Fig. 5 shows that linear operations take
roughly 80% of VLA execution time and are dominated by dense
matrix multiplications using Tensor cores. In contrast, MPC compu-
tation executes on general-purpose CUDA cores. This makes linear
operations suitable for fine-grained VLA-MPC co-location. There-
fore, when MPC overlaps with a linear operation, Dubot considers
all three mechanisms from Sec. 4.3. The final mechanism and its
resource configuration are determined by the co-location optimizer
in Sec. 5 based on the workload characteristics and target GPU.
Other Operations. In contrast, attention and non-linear opera-
tions are less suitable for fine-grained co-location with MPC on the
same SM. Although attention leverages Tensor-core computation,
it also places high pressure on memory bandwidth and shared mem-
ory. On the other hand, non-linear operations primarily execute on
general-purpose CUDA cores and thus compete directly with MPC
for the same execution resources. In both cases, sharing an SM with
MPC can introduce resource contention. Dubot therefore only uses
spatial partitioning when MPC overlaps with these operators.
In summary, Dubot considers all three mechanisms for linear
operations. For attention and non-linear operations, Dubot restricts
co-location to spatial partitioning to reduce SM resource contention.
Next, we describe how different MPC algorithms are divided into
small execution chunks and co-located with VLA operations.
QP-Based MPC Partitioning. As described in Sec. 2.3, QP-
based MPC refines a control sequence through an iterative solver.
Because each iteration depends on the output of the previous one,
the iterations must preserve their original execution order. To make
the QP workload predictable for co-location, Dubot executes each
MPC invocation with a fixed iteration budget. This budget is suf-
ficient for the QP problems to converge at the scales in our EAI
workloads. Dubot then groups consecutive QP iterations into small
chunks and co-locates one chunk of iterations with a VLA opera-
tion. The optimizer in Sec. 5 determines the number of QP iterations
assigned to each operation and its co-location mechanism.
MPPI-Based MPC Partitioning. Unlike QP-based MPC, MPPI-
based MPC evaluates a fixed number of sampled control paths.

Because different paths are mutually independent, they can be eval-
uated in parallel. Dubot then partitions the sampled paths into
groups and co-locates each path group with a VLA operator. The
paths within a group are distributed across GPU threads, allowing
their evaluation to overlap with VLA operations. The co-location op-
timizer in Sec. 5 determines how many sampled paths are scheduled
within each VLA operator and selects the corresponding co-location
mechanism based on the VLA operator and GPU resources.
5
Co-Location Optimization
Our co-location strategy in Sec. 4 exposes opportunities to overlap
VLA with high-frequency MPC kernels. However, the optimal co-
location schedule depends on multiple factors, e.g., the VLA model,
MPC algorithm, target control frequency, and GPU platform. To
address this trade-off, Dubot formulates VLA-MPC co-location as
a constrained optimization problem. The optimizer minimizes VLA
inference latency while enforcing the control deadline of every
MPC invocation as a hard QoS constraint. Sec. 5.1 first introduces
our analytical performance models. Sec. 5.2 then uses these models
to determine the co-location configuration of each VLA stage and
the mapping of MPC computation across the VLA timeline.
5.1
Performance Modeling
To optimize VLA-MPC co-location, Dubot requires latency esti-
mates for its standalone and co-located GPU executions. We there-
fore calibrate analytical models offline for each target GPU.
Standalone Linear Layer Kernels. We first describe the stan-
dalone latency model for VLA linear layers, which take the majority
of VLA execution time and are the primary target for fine-grained
co-location. Other VLA operators, e.g., attention and non-linear
operations, can be modeled using the same methodology. The stan-
dalone latency of the 𝑖th linear layer kernel, 𝑡𝑉
linear,𝑖, is,
𝑡𝑉

with the matrix dimensions. Based on these offline profiling results,
we can estimate the standalone latency of linear kernels.

through an iterative solver. To make its workload size predictable,
Dubot sets a fixed iteration budget for each MPC invocation. We
use a budget of 80 iterations, which was sufficient for convergence
on the evaluated QP instances (Fig. 11). For performance modeling,
we use the number of consecutive QP iterations as the input size of
a standalone QP batch (Fig. 12a). We then model the latency of a

5.2

With the performance models in Sec. 5.1, we formulate VLA-MPC
co-location as a constrained optimization problem. For clarity, the
window covers one VLA inference and its associated MPC jobs. The
formulation can naturally extend to multiple VLA inference steps.

Finally, every MPC invocation must satisfy its control deadline:
𝐶𝑗≤𝑑𝑗,
∀𝑗.
(30)
This constraint enforces the control deadlines under the modeled
execution times. If the admitted jobs cannot be placed within their
deadlines using the available stages, the formulation reports the
window as infeasible. A runtime deadline guarantee requires con-
servative latency bounds covering execution variability.
6
Experimental Setup
Evaluation Platforms. We evaluate Dubot on two Nvidia mobile
GPU platforms: Jetson AGX Orin [50] and Jetson AGX Thor [51].
Jetson AGX Orin has an Ampere mobile GPU with 275 TOPS of peak
performance. Jetson AGX Thor integrates a Blackwell mobile GPU
and delivers 2070 TOPS peak performance. Both platforms integrate
Tensor cores and CUDA cores, while Thor provides additional hard-
ware features for warp specialization. During the measurement,
Nvidia Orin and Thor SoCs run at 1.30 and 1.53 GHz, respectively.
Their power modes are 60 W and 120 W, respectively. VLA models
run at BF16 precision, while MPC algorithms run at FP32 precision.
Algorithms. We evaluate Dubot with three representative VLA
models covering three inference paradigms described in Sec. 2.2:
OpenVLA [36], OpenVLA-OFT [37], and UVA [40]. OpenVLA uses
an autoregressive inference paradigm, OpenVLA-OFT performs
PO-based inference, and UVA adopts a diffusion-based inference
paradigm. As shown in Tbl. 1, these models represent different VLA
execution patterns and provide a comprehensive evaluation.
Algorithm Implementation. To support the three co-location
mechanisms in Sec. 4.3, we customized our CUDA kernels. Although
(a) VLA latency on an Nvidia Orin SoC. (b) VLA latency on an Nvidia Thor SoC.
Fig. 14: The absolute latency of different VLA models in
cuBLAS, CUTLASS, and our implementation.
cuBLAS and CUTLASS provide off-the-shelf GEMM implementa-
tions, they cannot directly support all the co-location mechanisms
required by Dubot. Fig. 14 compares the inference latency of our im-
plementation against cuBLAS and CUTLASS on Orin and Thor SoCs.
Our implementation achieves comparable performance across VLA
models and GPU platforms. For MPC algorithms, we implement
the QP-based and MPPI-based solvers based on the open-source
cuOSQP [60] and MPPI-Generic [70] implementations, respectively.
Optimizer Implementation. We implement our co-location
optimization from Sec. 5 in Python with about 1k lines of code.
Then, we leverage the Google optimization library OR-Tools [15] to
solve the constrained optimization problem.
Software Setup. We evaluate the VLA models on two robotic
datasets: LIBERO [41] and PushT [19]. For closed-loop execution,
we integrate MPC with the MuJoCo simulator [69], where the opti-
mized control commands are applied to the simulated robot and the
updated states are fed back to MPC. VLA and MPC execute asyn-
chronously, with MPC using the latest available VLA-generated
reference. We report three metrics: (1) end-to-end latency of each
VLA-MPC control cycle, (2) energy consumption during execution,
and (3) MPC QoS hit rate, defined as the fraction of MPC jobs
whose control results are available by their deadlines. Unless oth-
erwise specified, MPC runs at a target frequency of 500 Hz [49],
and each MPC job is due 2 ms after its periodic release. Here, we
report speedup relative to the sequential execution baseline. The
co-location latency includes waiting for the completion of the out-
standing MPC jobs and the final reduction time in MPPI. We also
compute GPU energy by integrating readings from the built-in GPU
power sensor over the test interval.
Baselines. Since there is no prior work targeting VLA-MPC
co-location directly, we implement several baselines based on prior
work. We compare Dubot with two sequential baselines and four
single-mechanism co-location baselines. For a fair comparison, all
four co-location baselines use the optimizer in Sec. 5 to determine
their execution configurations and MPC-to-VLA mappings, but are
restricted to a single co-location mechanism. In contrast, Dubot
considers all available mechanisms and selects the most suitable
configuration for each VLA stage.
• CPU: This baseline executes VLA inference on the GPU and
MPC computation on the CPU of the same SoC. Here, VLA
and MPC are executed sequentially.
• Base: This baseline executes VLA inference and MPC com-
putation sequentially on the GPU with no co-location.
• Spatial: This baseline implements a spatial partitioning ap-
proach similar to prior work [77] by partitioning the GPU
at the SM level and assigning different SM groups to VLA
inference and MPC computation.
9


--- Page 10 ---
ISCA ’27, June 5–9, 2027, Atlanta, Georgia, USA
Zeyu Guo et al.
QP
MPPI
Fig. 15: Comparison of performance and normalized energy
among different baselines on an Orin SoC. Numbers are nor-
malized to Base. ‘S’: speedup; ‘E’: normalized energy.
QP
MPPI
Fig. 16: Comparison of performance and normalized energy
among different baselines on a Thor SoC. Numbers are nor-
malized to Base. ‘S’: speedup; ‘E’: normalized energy.
• Stream: This baseline adopts block-level co-location by exe-
cuting VLA and MPC as separate kernels in different CUDA
streams. Their thread blocks can share an SM when sufficient
resources are available.
• WASP-Limited: This baseline performs intra-block fusion
by partitioning threads within a block into different groups,
similar to prior work, Tacker [86]. We only report its perfor-
mance on Orin in our evaluation.
• WASP: This approach uses warp specialization [9] to as-
sign different warps within a block to dedicated tasks. It
also supports register reallocation (setmaxnreg) [53] and
asynchronous Tensor core execution [54]. Note that these
features are only supported by the Nvidia Thor SoC; we only
report its performance on Thor in our evaluation.
• Dubot: Our proposed framework considers all three co-
location mechanisms. It automatically selects the most suit-
able mechanism for each VLA stage using our optimizer.
7
Evaluation
7.1
Performance
Performance on Orin. Fig. 15 compares the performance and
energy savings of Dubot against different baselines on an Nvidia
Orin SoC. All results are normalized to Base, i.e., the GPU sequential
execution baseline. Compared with Base, Spatial provides limited
speedup (1.21×) because it maps VLA and MPC computations onto
different SM groups and cannot simultaneously utilize Tensor cores
and CUDA cores within the same SM.
Intra-block fusion approaches, e.g., WASP-Limited, can better
overlap the computation between the Tensor cores and CUDA
cores. On average, WASP-Limited achieves 1.27× speedup. How-
ever, WASP-Limited on Orin still suffers from the extra overhead
due to limited hardware support for warp specialization.
Dubot achieves the highest speedup across different EAI pipelines,
with up to 1.41× speedup. This is because Dubot can choose dif-
ferent co-location mechanisms for different operators. Moreover,
Dubot achieves the highest energy efficiency among the others.
Dubot reduces energy consumption by 16.1% compared with Base.
Performance on Thor. Fig. 16 compares the performance and
energy efficiency of Dubot with various baselines on the Thor SoC.
QP
MPPI
(a) QoS comparison on an Nvidia Orin SoC.
(b) QoS comparison on an Nvidia Thor SoC.
QP
MPPI
Fig. 17: The QoS Comparison among different baselines on
two mobile SoCs. The default MPC frequency is 500 Hz.
QP
MPPI
QP

(a) Nvidia Orin SoC.
(b) Nvidia Thor SoC.
Fig. 18: The breakdown of co-location mechanisms selected
by Dubot on two mobile SoCs.
(a) Nvidia Orin SoC.
(b) Nvidia Thor SoC.
Fig. 19: Ablation study on our co-location optimizer.
All performance results are normalized to Base. Here, we include
an additional baseline, WASP, which exploits newer architectural
support for warp-specialized execution. Overall, WASP achieves the
second-highest performance, 1.27× speedup over Base. Neverthe-
less, Dubot still outperforms other baselines with 1.35× speedup.
For energy savings, Dubot reduces GPU energy by 12.4% on Thor.
QoS. Fig. 17 compares the MPC QoS achieved by different base-
lines on two Nvidia SoCs, Orin and Thor, at a target control fre-
quency of 500 Hz. Because Base sequentially executes the VLA
inference and MPC computations, Base frequently delays MPC
execution behind VLA inference, achieving only 61.7% of QoS on
Orin and 63.7% on Thor, on average. In contrast, all co-location
baselines largely improve QoS by overlapping the two workloads.
On both Orin and Thor SoCs, Dubot achieves the best QoS, with
over 99% of QoS across all VLA models and MPC algorithms.
Mechanism Breakdown. Fig. 18 shows the breakdown of co-
location mechanisms selected by Dubot across different VLAs and
MPCs. On Orin, Stream and WASP-Limited account for 45.8% and
35.3% of the selections on average, respectively. On Thor, both
Stream and WASP are frequently selected, with WASP benefiting
from additional hardware support for warp specialization. Thus,
different VLA operators favor different co-location mechanisms.
7.2
Ablation Study
In this subsection, we evaluate the contribution of our optimizer by
replacing it with three heuristics. Uniform distributes QP iterations
as evenly as possible across VLA operators. Latency Proportional
(LP) assigns iterations in proportion to each operator’s standalone
latency. Gimbal is a greedy co-location algorithm [79]. Each base-
line can select the best-performing co-location mechanism for its

(a) VLA with QP-based MPC.
(b) VLA with MPPI-based MPC.
Fig. 20: The sensitivity of performance to predictive horizon
with two MPC solvers, QP and MPPI, on an Orin SoC. The
default MPC frequency is 500 Hz.
(a) VLA with QP-based MPC.
(b) VLA with MPPI-based MPC.
Fig. 21: The sensitivity of performance to MPC frequency
with two types of MPC solvers, QP-based and MPPI-based,
on Orin SoC. The default predictive horizon length is 50. The
speedup is normalized to the corresponding GPU baseline.
fixed QP assignment. Here, we only evaluate the QP-based MPC
algorithm over three VLA models.
In Fig. 19, LP consistently outperforms Uniform. This shows
that standalone VLA latency is a useful signal for workload place-
ment. Nevertheless, Dubot achieves the highest speedup for all
three VLA models on both Jetson Orin and Thor, even compared
with Gimbal. Dubot speedup ranges from 1.33× to 1.46×. Overall,
Dubot outperforms all heuristic methods across configurations.
7.3
Sensitivity Study
Predictive Horizon. Fig. 20 shows the sensitivity of speedup to the
MPC predictive horizon on the Orin SoC with a target frequency of
500 Hz. The length of the MPC predictive horizon is proportional
to the MPC workload. Here, we choose OpenVLA-OFT as a case
study. For both QP-based and MPPI-based MPC, as the predictive
horizon increases, the performance of all co-location strategies ini-
tially improves. This is because a larger MPC workload exposes
more opportunities to overlap with VLA inference. However, the
speedup eventually saturates and slightly decreases at larger hori-
zon windows as the MPC workload begins to exceed the overlap
window and dominates the execution latency. Both Spatial and
WASP-Limited show moderate speedup. Overall, Dubot achieves
1.3× average speedup when the horizon is between 30 and 70.
MPC Target Frequency. Fig. 21a and Fig. 21b show the sensitiv-
ity of speedup to the MPC target frequency on an Orin SoC, using
two MPC solvers: QP-based and MPPI-based. The default predic-
tive horizon length is 50. All numbers are normalized to the GPU
baseline. Here, we also use OpenVLA-OFT. For the QP-based solver
(Fig. 21a), all co-location approaches maintain a stable increase
in speedup in the frequency range from 100 to 500 Hz. Overall,
Dubot achieves roughly 1.3× speedup on average. For MPPI, as
the frequency increases, the trend is similar.
QP
MPPI
Fig. 22: Scalability study of Dubot with two different MPC
solvers, QP-based and MPPI-based, on an Orin SoC. Here, we
show four different robot types: a single-arm manipulator, a
quadruped robot, a dual-arm manipulator, and a humanoid.
Speedup is normalized to the corresponding GPU baseline.
7.4
Case Study
To evaluate the generality of Dubot, we measure its performance
across four representative robot platforms: a single-arm manipula-
tor, a quadruped robot, a dual-arm robot, and a humanoid. To mimic
the workloads of different robot platforms, we fix the workload of
the VLA model and use OpenVLA-OFT as a case study. We then em-
ulate MPC workloads derived from four robot configurations. These
robot configurations are derived from the reported specifications
and degrees of freedom of the platforms [24, 25, 30, 35].
Fig. 22a and Fig. 22b show the speedup and normalized energy of
different co-location variants on the Orin SoC with two MPC solvers,
QP-based and MPPI-based. The performance numbers are normal-
ized to the corresponding GPU baselines. Across all four robot types,
Dubot consistently achieves the highest speedup, roughly 1.4×.
The speedup of Dubot remains stable because Dubot’s co-location
optimizer automatically adapts the mapping of the available GPU
resources between VLA kernels and MPC computations.
For energy savings, Dubot also achieves the best energy effi-
ciency across all robot platforms. It reduces energy consumption
by roughly 20% compared to Base. On the other hand, Spatial
provides only modest energy improvement, as statically splitting
SMs between the two workloads can lead to idle compute units on
both partitions. Overall, the results show that Dubot generalizes
effectively across diverse robot types without manual tuning.
8
Related Work
MPC Acceleration. MPC is a key component in robotic systems
and has received extensive attention from the architecture commu-
nity [1, 21, 48, 49, 59, 68, 73, 80]. For instance, RoboX [59] targets the
conventional robotic MPC pipeline, while RSQP [73] accelerates its
underlying quadratic programs. Others [21, 68] target optimization-
based robotic workloads. Robomorphic [49], RoboShape [48], and
Dadu-RBD [80] accelerate rigid-body dynamics, whereas Tartan [1]
designs a programmable processor for robotic control.
However, existing techniques primarily treat MPC as an iso-
lated workload and optimize its efficiency. Dubot explores the
computational characteristics between MPC and VLA, and designs
a co-location framework on off-the-shelf GPUs.
VLA Acceleration. Recent VLA acceleration methods mainly
focus on algorithmic optimization. Some [42, 74, 83, 89] reduce
inference cost through compression and quantization techniques.
Others [81, 84] dynamically skip unnecessary layers or decoding
steps for similar inputs. Token-pruning approaches [67, 72, 78] re-
move redundant visual tokens while preserving task-level precision.
Recently, there have been some algorithm-hardware co-designs for
11


--- Page 12 ---
ISCA ’27, June 5–9, 2027, Atlanta, Georgia, USA
Zeyu Guo et al.
VLA [44, 57, 64]. Different from these approaches that reduce the
cost of VLA inference alone, Dubot focuses on system-level opti-
mization to improve end-to-end EAI performance on mobile GPUs.
Kernel Fusion and Co-Location. Recent kernel fusion tech-
niques reduce execution overhead by combining operators, mini-
mizing intermediate memory traffic and kernel launches [79, 85–87].
Some [6, 88, 91] enable compiler-driven fusion via tensor sched-
uling. Others propose various techniques to manage interference
between GPU workloads [20, 66]. Further, studies [27, 34, 55, 58] ex-
plore domain-specific optimization and communication. In contrast,
Dubot performs robotics-specific optimization via co-location.
Autonomous System Acceleration. Recent architectural re-
search has explored a broad range of techniques to accelerate
robotic systems [5, 8, 31, 32, 38, 39, 43, 61, 62, 71]. Some mainly focus
on optimizing individual components in robotics, such as localiza-
tion [31, 39, 43] and collision detection [61, 62]. Recent architectural
efforts have begun targeting embodied AI and autonomous driv-
ing [5, 8, 32, 71]. Dubot also speeds up the VLA-MPC loops via
co-optimizing its algorithms holistically.
9
Conclusion
Future EAI will not be defined solely by larger foundation mod-
els, but by how effectively the high-level planning loop and the
low-level control loop are integrated and executed together. This
integration also calls for a new generation of EAI architectures that
jointly optimize model design, runtime system, and architecture.
